name: Turmeric root extract
lead: Turmeric root extract is a preparation made from the rhizome of Curcuma longa, a plant of the ginger family. Its main colored constituent is curcumin, a yellow polyphenol that is also used as a food coloring, a dietary supplement ingredient and a cosmetic ingredient.[1] In skincare it is marketed mainly as a brightening or antioxidant ingredient.

Laboratory work has examined curcumin and turmeric extract in skin-cell models, for example a 2023 cell-culture study combining turmeric root extract with another antioxidant in keratinocytes exposed to ultraviolet light.[2] No clinical trial of topical turmeric root extract for skin brightening or complexion appears among the sources reviewed for this entry. Wikipedia's curcumin article states that extensive studies have not established medical value for curcumin, citing its instability and poor absorption, and also lists it as a contact allergen.[1]
infobox: Cosmetic and food ingredient; FDA-approved food coloring; E100 in the EU[1]

paras: Turmeric is the ground or extracted root of Curcuma longa. Curcumin is a diarylheptanoid polyphenol that dissolves poorly in water but readily in organic solvents, and it binds metal ions such as iron and copper.[1] Extracts are sold for culinary use, as supplements and as cosmetic ingredients, and also appear in combination products, including joint supplements listed on US drug-label databases.[3]

Product listings describe turmeric root extract as a skin-brightening ingredient, often alongside other plant extracts. The sources reviewed here do not include published human data on whether topical use changes skin tone or pigmentation.

No studies found for topical turmeric root extract as a skin-brightening or cosmetic agent. Related laboratory research is limited to cell models: curcumin suppressed TGF-beta signaling in fibroblasts taken from scleroderma patients,[4] and a combination of turmeric root extract and dimethylmethoxy chromanol reduced ultraviolet-induced oxidative damage in a human keratinocyte line.[2] These cell studies did not test skin brightening in people. Human trials registered for turmeric or curcumin concern oral use for other conditions.

Wikipedia reports that curcumin is a contact allergen, may interact with prescription drugs and that reported oral side effects include nausea, diarrhea, hives and dizziness; it also records cases of liver injury linked to curcumin supplements.[1] A 2015 case report described yellow discoloration of the feet in a patient who took turmeric orally.[5] Curcumin is a strong yellow pigment, and staining of skin or fabric is a recognized property of the compound.

card.summary: Curcumin-rich plant extract sold as a skin brightener; evidence for that use is limited to cell studies.
card.note: Contact allergen; strongly pigmented and can stain.

quick.overview:
Turmeric root extract comes from the Curcuma longa rhizome and is used in cosmetics as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient. Its main pigment is curcumin.

The sources reviewed here contain no human trials of topical turmeric extract for skin tone. Research is limited to cell-culture experiments.
quick.mechanism: In laboratory cell models curcumin has been reported to dampen TGF-beta signaling and, combined with another antioxidant, to reduce UV-induced oxidative damage in keratinocytes. Whether this translates to visible brightening in people has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Curcumin is listed as a contact allergen and a strong yellow pigment. Oral use has been linked to side effects such as nausea and, rarely, liver injury, and a case report describes yellow discoloration of the feet. It is an approved food coloring in the US and E100 in the EU.
